title: Symfony Exercises
description: Read each example in its lesson first. Predict the result, then check your answer. The notes explain the idea and one common mistake.

exercises.code:
<?php
namespace App\Controller;
use Symfony\Bundle\FrameworkBundle\Controller\AbstractController;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Request;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\JsonResponse;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\RedirectResponse;
use Symfony\Component\Routing\Attribute\Route;
class LessonController extends AbstractController {
#[Route("/hello", methods: ["GET"])]
public function hello(): Response { return new Response("Hello, Asha!"); }
}
exercises.question: A Route attribute maps a URL to a controller method. Open GET /hello. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: The Route attribute chooses GET /hello. The returned Response contains its greeting text. Keep the attribute above the method it describes.

exercises.code:
<?php
namespace App\Controller;
use Symfony\Bundle\FrameworkBundle\Controller\AbstractController;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Request;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\JsonResponse;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\RedirectResponse;
use Symfony\Component\Routing\Attribute\Route;
class LessonController extends AbstractController {
#[Route("/book", methods: ["GET"])]
public function book(): JsonResponse { return new JsonResponse(["title" => "Moon Trip", "pages" => 24]); }
}
exercises.question: JsonResponse turns an array into JSON and sets its content type. Open GET /book. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: JsonResponse serialises the associative array with title and pages fields. Use JsonResponse rather than hand-building JSON strings.

exercises.code:
<?php
namespace App\Controller;
use Symfony\Bundle\FrameworkBundle\Controller\AbstractController;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Request;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\JsonResponse;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\RedirectResponse;
use Symfony\Component\Routing\Attribute\Route;
class LessonController extends AbstractController {
#[Route("/hello/{name}", methods: ["GET"])]
public function hello(string $name): Response { return new Response("Hi, " . $name . "!", 200, ["Content-Type" => "text/plain"]); }
}
exercises.question: A route placeholder can become a method input. Open GET /hello/Ravi. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: The placeholder value becomes the method input. The content type makes the reply plain text. Treat route inputs as untrusted text.

exercises.code:
<?php
namespace App\Controller;
use Symfony\Bundle\FrameworkBundle\Controller\AbstractController;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Request;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\JsonResponse;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\RedirectResponse;
use Symfony\Component\Routing\Attribute\Route;
class LessonController extends AbstractController {
#[Route("/search", methods: ["GET"])]
public function search(Request $request): JsonResponse { return new JsonResponse(["term" => $request->query->get("q", "")]); }
}
exercises.question: A Request object gives access to query values. Open GET /search?q=cat. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: The query bag reads q from the Request. The JsonResponse puts cat under term. Check client values before using them in a database query or file path.

exercises.code:
<?php
namespace App\Controller;
use Symfony\Bundle\FrameworkBundle\Controller\AbstractController;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Request;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\JsonResponse;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\RedirectResponse;
use Symfony\Component\Routing\Attribute\Route;
class LessonController extends AbstractController {
#[Route("/double/{n}", requirements: ["n" => "[0-9]+"], methods: ["GET"])]
public function twice(int $n): JsonResponse { return new JsonResponse(["answer" => $n * 2]); }
}
exercises.question: A route requirement describes allowed path text. Open GET /double/4. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: The route requirement allows the digits in 4. Symfony supplies the typed input to the method. A requirement controls route matching, not every allowed data range.

exercises.code:
<?php
namespace App\Controller;
use Symfony\Bundle\FrameworkBundle\Controller\AbstractController;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Request;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\JsonResponse;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\RedirectResponse;
use Symfony\Component\Routing\Attribute\Route;
class LessonController extends AbstractController {
#[Route("/books", methods: ["POST"])]
public function create(Request $request): JsonResponse {
 $data = $request->toArray();
 if (!is_string($data["title"] ?? null)) return new JsonResponse(["error" => "Title needed"], 400);
 return new JsonResponse(["title" => $data["title"]], 201);
}
}
exercises.question: Request::toArray reads JSON into an array. Send POST /books with application/json and {"title":"Moon Trip"}. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: toArray parses the JSON body. The title type check passes and a 201 reply is built. Malformed JSON can fail before your own field checks run.

exercises.code:
<?php
namespace App\Controller;
use Symfony\Bundle\FrameworkBundle\Controller\AbstractController;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Request;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\JsonResponse;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\RedirectResponse;
use Symfony\Component\Routing\Attribute\Route;
class LessonController extends AbstractController {
#[Route("/hello/{name}", name: "hello", methods: ["GET"])]
public function hello(string $name): Response { return new Response($name); }
#[Route("/link", methods: ["GET"])]
public function link(): Response { return new Response($this->generateUrl("hello", ["name" => "Asha"])); }
}
exercises.question: A route name lets code build a link without repeating its path. Open GET /link. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: generateUrl looks up the hello name and substitutes Asha into its path. The parameter key must match the placeholder.

exercises.code:
<?php
namespace App\Controller;
use Symfony\Bundle\FrameworkBundle\Controller\AbstractController;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Request;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\JsonResponse;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\RedirectResponse;
use Symfony\Component\Routing\Attribute\Route;
class LessonController extends AbstractController {
#[Route("/start", methods: ["GET"])]
public function start(): RedirectResponse { return new RedirectResponse("/hello"); }
#[Route("/hello", methods: ["GET"])]
public function hello(): Response { return new Response("Welcome"); }
}
exercises.question: RedirectResponse tells a client where to request next. GET /start ends at /hello in a browser. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: RedirectResponse sends a location. The second request calls hello and receives Welcome. A redirect starts a new client request.

exercises.code:
<?php
namespace App\Controller;
use Symfony\Bundle\FrameworkBundle\Controller\AbstractController;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Request;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\JsonResponse;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\RedirectResponse;
use Symfony\Component\Routing\Attribute\Route;
class LessonController extends AbstractController {
#[Route("/missing", methods: ["GET"])]
public function missing(): JsonResponse { return new JsonResponse(["error" => "Book not found"], 404); }
}
exercises.question: The second JsonResponse argument is the status. Open GET /missing. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: The response constructor takes both the error data and the 404 status. Do not hide a missing item behind a 200 success status.

exercises.code:
<?php
namespace App\Controller;
use Symfony\Bundle\FrameworkBundle\Controller\AbstractController;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Request;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\JsonResponse;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\RedirectResponse;
use Symfony\Component\Routing\Attribute\Route;
class LessonController extends AbstractController {
#[Route("/note", methods: ["GET"])]
public function note(): Response { $response = new Response("Practice note"); $response->headers->set("Cache-Control", "no-store"); return $response; }
}
exercises.question: A Response has a header bag. Open GET /note and inspect Cache-Control. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: The header bag is edited before the Response is returned. Headers and body are separate parts of a response.

exercises.code:
<?php
namespace App\Controller;
use Symfony\Bundle\FrameworkBundle\Controller\AbstractController;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Request;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\JsonResponse;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\RedirectResponse;
use Symfony\Component\Routing\Attribute\Route;
class LessonController extends AbstractController {
#[Route("/ready", methods: ["GET"])]
public function ready(): Response { return new Response("Ready"); }
}
exercises.question: The methods option limits which requests match. GET /ready gives this reply; POST is not allowed. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: The attribute admits GET requests. A different HTTP method does not enter this handler. Use the correct HTTP method for the operation.

exercises.code:
<?php
namespace App\Controller;
use Symfony\Bundle\FrameworkBundle\Controller\AbstractController;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Request;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\JsonResponse;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\RedirectResponse;
use Symfony\Component\Routing\Attribute\Route;
class LessonController extends AbstractController {
#[Route("/books", methods: ["GET"])]
public function books(): JsonResponse { return new JsonResponse(["Moon Trip", "Sun Trip"]); }
}
exercises.question: A PHP list becomes a JSON array. Open GET /books. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: The PHP list contains two strings, so the JSON reply has two array items. A JSON list has ordered items; an object has named fields.
